title: The Goat Shed and the Beggar Bar: Berlin, the Grotesque Dance, and Four Rooms Taken Away
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Berlin, birth in the merchant's house
stops.date_confidence: attested. The birth address was not located in any reachable source, so the stop sits at the central Berlin pin rather than at a street.
stops.campa: Gertrud Valesca Samosch is born in Berlin, eldest child of Theodor Samosch, a merchant tied to the firm Zade und Falk, and Augusta Samosch, born Rosenthal. The house is prosperous and assimilated, Jewish in the registry more than in the practice. Her mother arranges ballet lessons while she is still small; the sources cannot agree whether the child is seven or nine when she begins, and none of them can name the street the family lived on. The registry gives the date, the eleventh of January 1892, and the parents' names, and after that the record of her childhood stops.
suggested_refs: The Samosch family's Berlin commercial milieu and the firm of Zade und Falk

stops.name: Berlin, the stage door and the lily of the valley
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Gert's own memoir, and contradicted three ways. She places the encounter in her childhood, about 1899 to 1901; Anna Pavlova's first Berlin appearances are generally dated 1908-09, and the year here is set to 1908 only to hold segment order. The theatre is unknown: the placeholder coordinate circulating for this episode, the Deutsches Opernhaus in Charlottenburg, is anachronistic, since that house did not open until 7 November 1912, and has been discarded in favour of the central Berlin pin. No source independent of the memoir was reached.
stops.campa: She waits at a stage door with her friend Else for the Russian to come out. Anna Pavlova, coming out, pulls a lily of the valley from her own bouquet and gives it to the child, who presses it into her diary and calls Pavlova, ever after, her third love. The record fixes neither the theatre nor the year, and Pavlova's Berlin dates will not sit still under the story. It survives because Gert wrote it down half a century later, in a book that reorders her life freely.
sources: Valeska Gert, Ich bin eine Hexe (1968), as summarized in the research dossier
anna_pavlova.journey.json, which carries no Berlin stop earlier than 1914
suggested_refs: Anna Pavlova's Berlin appearances, generally dated from 1908 onward

stops.name: Berlin, Moissi, Breiderhoff, Sacchetto
stops.date_confidence: attested for about 1915; no month is recorded and no address of study is given by any source. The remark on Isadora Duncan comes from the dossier's summary of Gert's own writing and was not traced to a printed page this pass.
stops.campa: She studies acting with Maria Moissi and Alfred Breiderhoff, and dance with Rita Sacchetto, whose company will hand her a stage. She is twenty-three, trained late and badly by ballet's arithmetic, and she has already decided that the trained body is the thing to attack. Isadora Duncan she credits with breaking ballet open; Duncan's return to Greek harmony she throws out as romantic, a prettier prison than the one before it. What she wants instead is the body under economic pressure: the whore, the procuress, the boxer, the coloratura, the dying.
suggested_refs: Isadora Duncan, 'The Dance of the Future', delivered in Berlin, 1903

segments.name: Tanz in Orange: The First Stages

stops.name: Berlin, Nollendorfplatz: Tanz in Orange
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln's programme-based work catalogue, which the archive itself calls provisional and whose URL now returns 404. Contradiction left open: an earlier showing a few days before, probably at the Apollo-Theater, is reported but not securely dated, and a third account names the Bluethner-Saal. Only the U.T. Lichtspiele date has a surviving programme behind it.
stops.campa: At the U.T. Lichtspiele on Nollendorfplatz she dances Tanz in Orange on a Rita Sacchetto programme: orange silk, the face whitened, the feet bare. Sacchetto has made the piece; Gert dances it as an argument against the making. It is the first appearance the archives can put a date on, and two other halls are named in two other accounts of the same fortnight, so even the beginning is contested. The room takes it for a novelty number on a variety bill. She keeps the dance in repertoire for five years.
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
suggested_refs: Rita Sacchetto's Berlin dance programmes of 1916

stops.name: Munich, the Kammerspiele engagement
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1916/17 season; the month is not recorded and is set to September to open the season.
stops.campa: Otto Falckenberg engages her at the Muenchner Kammerspiele for the season. It is a proper contract in a proper theatre, the only kind of employment she will ever hold for any length of time, and it teaches her precisely what she will spend the rest of her life refusing: entrances, cues, a director's blocking, a part somebody else has written down. Bavaria is in the third year of the war and the houses are full of people who want an evening off. She takes the wages and works the late nights elsewhere.
suggested_refs: Otto Falckenberg's wartime seasons at the Muenchner Kammerspiele

stops.name: Munich, the Bonbonniere and the dance caricatures
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1917; the day is not recorded, and the Bonbonniere's exact street address was not located, so the coordinate approximates the Munich cabaret district. The October 1917 programme of new dances at the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten on Maximilianstrasse is separately attested and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In the cabaret she is free of the play. She calls the pieces dance caricatures and that is exactly what they are: a person cut down to the three or four movements that person cannot stop making. A waiter, a soldier, a woman on a corner, each reduced to a tic and repeated until the room stops laughing. In October she carries new dances into the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten on Maximilianstrasse, a hall of an altogether more respectable order, and the caricatures work there too.
suggested_refs: The Bonbonniere, Munich, and the wartime Kabarett circuit

stops.name: Bucharest, the first foreign tour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The tour with Erik Charell appears in the dossier's summary of Frank-Manuel Peter's documentary biography and in no source reached independently this pass; the coordinate marks central Bucharest only, and the month is the dossier's.
stops.campa: She travels to Bucharest with the theatre director Erik Charell, the first time her work leaves German-speaking ground. Romania is under German occupation and the punitive treaty is signed in the city that spring, so the audience is partly an army. Nothing survives of what she danced there, or in which hall, or to whom. The tour is a line in Frank-Manuel Peter's biography of her. No programme, no notice, and no date more exact than the month has been found.
sources: Frank-Manuel Peter's documentary biography, as summarized in the research dossier
suggested_refs: Erik Charell's wartime touring companies

segments.name: The Expressionist Stages and the Prostitute's Dance

stops.name: Berlin, the marriage to Helmuth von Krause
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedias.
stops.campa: She marries the physician Helmuth von Krause, son of the Prussian jurist and politician Paul von Krause. The match sets a stage grotesque inside a family of the imperial legal establishment, eight months before the empire stops existing. They stay married on paper for seventeen years, through her long relationship with the actor Aribert Wascher and through the whole of her Weimar career. The divorce will not be finalized until November 1935, by which time a Jewish wife has become a danger to a German husband, and the paper is worth something else entirely.
suggested_refs: Paul von Krause, Prussian jurist and Reich minister of justice, the bridegroom's father

stops.name: Berlin, the Deutsches Theater: Kokoschka's Hiob
stops.date_confidence: the year 1918 is attested on German Wikipedia; the month is not established and is set to October. Widely reported, no primary document reached. Coordinate corrected to the Deutsches Theater at Schumannstrasse 13a, 52.5244, 13.3819; a figure of 52.5258, 13.3874 in circulation falls about 410 m northeast, across the Charite grounds.
stops.campa: Max Reinhardt takes her into the Deutsches Theater and its Kammerspiele, and she appears in Oskar Kokoschka's Hiob, a play in which a head comes off and a woman falls through the ceiling. She is inside the best-run theatre in Germany, playing the most violent text available to it. Reinhardt's house is where a German career gets made. Hers goes the other way: within a year she is dancing alone in rented concert halls where the programme is whatever she says it is and nobody else's name is on the bill.
suggested_refs: Oskar Kokoschka's Hiob and the Reinhardt Kammerspiele repertoire of 1918

stops.name: Hamburg, the Weisser Saal: Canaille
stops.date_confidence: the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln's programme-based catalogue gives this date and hall; that catalogue is described as provisional by the archive itself and its URL now returns 404. Contradiction unresolved: English Wikipedia and most secondary summaries place the premiere and the notoriety of Canaille in the early 1920s, and some summaries date the piece to 1915 or 1916. The exact address of the Weisser Saal was not located.
stops.campa: Ten weeks after the empire falls she premieres Canaille in Hamburg. A prostitute displays herself, transacts, and pauses in exhaustion. The dance runs the whole of the labour through in a few minutes and ends on the contempt rather than on the act. She performs it in a black skirt cut very short over long black stockings and heels. The body on the stage is being used for money at the speed money uses it, and when the transaction is done the body spits and wanders off.
stops.quote: Provocatively I wiggle my hips, lift the very short, black skirt, show white thigh flesh over long, black silk stockings and high-heeled shoes... I am a sensitive prostitute, moving softly and lustfully... I sink slowly in the knees, open the legs wide and sink deeply. In every spasm, as if bitten by a tarantella, I twitch in the air... What had the man done to me? He used my body, because I needed money. Miserable world! I spit contemptuously, stepping to the right and to the left, then wandered off.
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Ich bin eine Hexe, pp. 47-48, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 43
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 43
suggested_refs: Fred Hildenbrandt, Die Taenzerin Valeska Gert (1928), source of the photograph captioned 'Pause'
Frank-Manuel Peter, 'Puck, Punk oder Pausen-Clown?' (2021), arguing the 'Pause' photograph shows a resting pose inside Canaille rather than a separate dance

stops.name: Berlin, Die Tribuene: Toller's Die Wandlung
stops.date_confidence: the premiere of Die Wandlung is attested to 30 September 1919 at Die Tribuene, Berlin, directed by Karlheinz Martin; Gert's appearance in the play is attested on English Wikipedia without a date. Correction to a common error: the play is often bundled into her Reinhardt engagement, which is wrong, since Die Tribuene was an independent expressionist house. No coordinate for Die Tribuene was established, so this stop uses the central Berlin pin.
stops.campa: Ernst Toller writes Die Wandlung in a cell and Karlheinz Martin stages it at Die Tribuene, a small independent house with no proscenium worth the name, while Toller is still serving time for the Munich republic. Gert is in it. The play is a returning soldier's conversion, shouted, and the acting it demands is the thing she has been building alone since Munich: no character, no arc, a body making an argument. For one autumn the German stage is doing what she does. Then it stops, and she goes back to renting halls.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Ernst Toller' (premiere date, house, and director)
suggested_refs: Karlheinz Martin's production of Die Wandlung at Die Tribuene, September 1919

stops.name: Baden-Baden, the last Tanz in Orange
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln catalogue as the final documented performance of the piece, with the provisional-catalogue caveat noted above. The exact address of the Staedtisches Schauspiel was not located.
stops.campa: At the Staedtisches Schauspiel in Baden-Baden she dances Tanz in Orange for the last time the record knows of. The piece is five years old, it is Sacchetto's and not hers, and it is the only thing in her repertoire that anyone would call pretty. She leaves it in the spa town and does not bring it back. Twenty-seven years later she will re-enter Germany through this same town, on a six-month permit issued by an army of occupation, with none of the intervening repertoire allowed to have happened.
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
suggested_refs: The Staedtisches Schauspiel, Baden-Baden, and its 1921 season

stops.name: Berlin, the Klindworth-Scharwenka-Saal: Salome cut down
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved and material. The Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln catalogue puts the premiere of her reduced Salome here on 26 November 1921; the dossier and other secondary summaries put it on 20 April 1923 at Berlin's Tribuene. Both cannot be the premiere; the catalogue URL returns 404 and the archive calls that catalogue provisional, so neither date can be preferred. The date used here holds segment order only. Coordinate corrected: the hall belonged to the Klindworth-Scharwenka-Konservatorium at Luetzowstrasse 76, Berlin-Tiergarten, 52.5040, 13.3583.
stops.campa: She takes Salome, an hour of orientalist scenery and Strauss and a full orchestra, and reduces it to a few minutes of one woman. No veils, no Herod, no head on a plate. The hall belongs to a conservatory and the audience has come out for concert music. This is the method she will keep for the rest of her working life: take the famous thing, strip off everything the fame is attached to, and dance what is left standing. Whether it happened in this hall in 1921 or two years later at the Tribuene, the sources will not say.
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
suggested_refs: The concert halls of the Klindworth-Scharwenka-Konservatorium, Luetzowstrasse 76

stops.name: Berlin, the audience calls the police
stops.date_confidence: tradition. English Wikipedia reports that when she danced Canaille with an orgasm in Berlin in 1922 the audience called the police, and gives no primary citation. Note the direction, which is often mis-stated: the audience summoned police. No source describes an intervention, a report, or a charge, and no contemporary police record was located. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: She dances the orgasm in Canaille in front of a Berlin audience and the audience telephones for the police. What the police did, whether they came at all, whether anything was ever written down, nobody has ever found out; the story circulates with no document under it, without a venue, a day of the month, or a policeman's name. Kurt Tucholsky, who is at the Weltbuehne and misses nothing, files her under the most impudent things ever done on a stage.
stops.quote: likely the most impudent of things ever to be done on stage
stops.quote_source: Kurt Tucholsky on Gert's stage work, in the English translation given on arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert'; the German original could not be checked, zeno.org being unreachable this pass
suggested_refs: Kurt Tucholsky's Weltbuehne notices of the Berlin dance season

stops.name: Berlin, the Schwechtensaal: Tod
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln catalogue, with the provisional-catalogue caveat; English Wikipedia gives November 1922 without a day. The exact address of the Schwechtensaal was not located.
stops.campa: A long black garment, a body breathing, a contraction, stillness, and the head going down at the end. That is the whole of Tod. She has reduced dance to physiological dying and set it on a concert programme between other numbers, so that an audience watches a woman stop, in real time, and then applauds. It is the one piece American critics will single out for praise eighteen years later in Greenwich Village, when everything else on the same programme strikes them as too European to follow.
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
suggested_refs: Wolfgang Mueller, ed., Valeska Gert. Bewegte Fragmente. Eine Quellenedition (2013), on the reception of the still and near-motionless pieces

segments.name: The Camera Learns to Hold Her

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, Puck and the fear of shooting
stops.date_confidence: the role of Puck under Hans Neumann and the hostility of the set are attested; the shooting location is not. No source names where Ein Sommernachtstraum was shot, and the Babelsberg pin is an inference from its being the principal Berlin-area studio complex of the period. A figure of 52.4064, 13.1372 in circulation for this stop falls about 3.1 km northeast of the lot, in open land. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Hans Neumann casts her as Puck and runs a set she afterwards describes as hostile to her. She cannot sleep. The camera is a machine that does not applaud, does not breathe, and does not stop when a thing has gone wrong, and she is a performer whose entire method is built on the room in front of her and its reaction second by second. Shakespeare's trickster of the wood, the fastest creature in the play, gets performed by a woman who has not slept and is frightened of the lens.
stops.quote: I was tired because the fear of shooting prevented me from sleeping.
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, quoted in silentfilm.org, 'A Pungent Presence: Valeska Gert in Silent Film'
sources: silentfilm.org, 'A Pungent Presence: Valeska Gert in Silent Film'
suggested_refs: Hans Neumann's Ein Sommernachtstraum (1925)

stops.name: Berlin, Frau Greifer in the joyless street
stops.date_confidence: the film, the role, the year and the casting alongside Asta Nielsen and Greta Garbo are attested; the shooting location is not. Die freudlose Gasse was a Sofar-Film production and no source found places its shooting at Neubabelsberg, so this stop uses the central Berlin pin rather than an invented studio. Month unknown, defaulted to May. The two later Pabst films named in the campa are attested to 1929 and 1931 respectively.
stops.campa: G. W. Pabst casts her in Die freudlose Gasse as Frau Greifer, the procuress who keeps a dress shop that is not a dress shop, in a Vienna starving through the inflation. Asta Nielsen is in it and so is a young Swede called Greta Garbo. The photographer Suse Byk works with her across the production until the fear turns over into its opposite. She will make two more films for Pabst: the sadistic reformatory director in Tagebuch einer Verlorenen, opposite Louise Brooks, and Frau Peachum in Die 3-Groschen-Oper.
stops.quote: pleasure in what had pained me before: being captured by the camera
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, quoted in silentfilm.org, 'A Pungent Presence: Valeska Gert in Silent Film'
sources: silentfilm.org, 'A Pungent Presence: Valeska Gert in Silent Film'
arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert' (screening the film, 11 July 2026)
suggested_refs: Suse Byk's studio portraits of Gert, made during the 1925 production

stops.name: Berlin, Nana's maid and the sound dances
stops.date_confidence: both items are attested to 1926; neither has a month, and January is a placeholder. The shooting location of Renoir's Nana is not established, so the stop uses the central Berlin pin.
stops.campa: Jean Renoir films Nana and she plays Zoe, the maid who watches the whole collapse from the doorway and keeps the door. The same year she begins the Tontaenze, the sound dances, in which the moving body acquires a voice that shrieks, chokes, gargles, and produces speech pulled deliberately out of shape. Sound film does not exist in Germany yet. She is making it on a stage, by mouth, three years early. No recording of the Tontaenze was ever made, and the only account of how they sounded is her own, in Mein Weg.
sources: arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert' (screening Nana, 10 July 2026)
suggested_refs: Jean Renoir's Nana (1926)
The Tontaenze, described in Gert's Mein Weg (1931)

stops.name: Paris, the Comedie des Champs-Elysees
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln catalogue, with the provisional-catalogue caveat noted above.
stops.campa: She brings Chansonette and Opus I, Komposition auf ausgeleiertem Klavier to the Comedie des Champs-Elysees. The second title tells the audience exactly what is coming: a composition for a piano gone out of tune and out of time, played not on the piano but by a body. Paris takes her, as Paris has been taking German exports of this kind for a decade. The Tanzarchiv's programme is the only record of the evening, and the archive calls its own catalogue provisional.
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Koeln, Valeska Gert work catalogue
suggested_refs: The Comedie des Champs-Elysees programmes of March 1930

stops.name: Kampen auf Sylt, the first sight of the island
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1930 by sylt.de; no month is given, and June is a placeholder. Coordinate corrected: Kampen is 54.954, 8.344; a figure of 54.9394, 8.3389 in circulation falls about 1.6 km south, in the dune belt outside the village. Note that sylt.de says only that she liked the place enough that a house was built for her, and does not say her husband had it built.
stops.campa: Friends recommend the island and she goes. Kampen is a village of thatched roofs on a sandbank in the North Sea, an hour of dunes from anything, with a light on the cliff and a beach where Berlin comes to take its clothes off. She likes it enough that a house gets built for her there. For twenty-one years it is a summer address and nothing more. Then Berlin runs out, twice, and the house becomes the whole of her territory: a bar, a stage, a kitchen, a bed, and the sea behind it.
suggested_refs: Kampen auf Sylt as a Weimar artists' resort

stops.name: Berlin, the Kohlkopp
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1932 and described as short-lived; no month is recorded, January is a placeholder, and no street address is given by any source.
stops.campa: She opens the first cabaret of her own and calls it the Kohlkopp, the Cabbage Head. It does not last, and no source records the street it stood on. For sixteen years she has been performing other people's programmes in other people's halls, and the discovery she makes here, in the last full year of the republic, is that she would rather own the room than be booked into it. Every venue she runs from now on will be taken away from her by an authority of one kind or another.
stops.quote: As I didn't love the citizen, I danced the roles of those he felt contempt for, the whores, the procuresses, those on the slide, those at the bottom.
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Mein Weg (1931), in the English translation given on arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert'
suggested_refs: Valeska Gert, Mein Weg (Leipzig, 1931)

segments.name: Entartet: The Passport and the Closing Door

stops.name: Berlin, declared degenerate
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was declared entartet and shut out of German stage and screen; the September date marks the exclusion of Jews from the Reich cultural chambers. Correction to a common overstatement: German Wikipedia records that she could still perform through the Kulturbund Deutscher Juden, so this is expulsion from the mainstream with one segregated outlet left, not a total ban on performing. The report that Goebbels's Das erwachende Berlin carried her photograph among the rejected Weimar theatre is dossier-only and unconfirmed. Mary Wigman's 1933 accommodation is attested in her own file; the Gert-Wigman rivalry comes from the dossier, and the Wigman file does not mention Gert.
stops.campa: She is attacked on two counts at once, as a Jew and as an artist of exactly the kind the new state files under degenerate, and by September the Reich cultural chambers are closed to Jews. What is left is the Kulturbund Deutscher Juden, a segregated association licensed to perform for Jewish audiences only. Mary Wigman, whose stamping and dust-raising Gert had been caricaturing for a decade as pseudo-classical, stays, takes a local office in the regime's dance-teachers league, and watches the Jewish names come off her own school's rolls.
sources: mary_wigman.journey.json, stop 'Dresden, the Gleichschaltung reaches the hill-house'
suggested_refs: The Kulturbund Deutscher Juden and the segregated performance economy after 1933

stops.name: London, Pett and Pott
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia's filmography lists '1934: Pett and Pott; Regie: Alberto Cavalcanti', and the Arsenal Berlin 2026 retrospective screens the film. No month is recorded and January is a placeholder. The item sits out of chronological order in most summaries, printed after the 1936 marriage.
stops.campa: Alberto Cavalcanti makes Pett and Pott for the GPO Film Unit, a sound experiment dressed up as a suburban fairy story about the telephone, and she is in it. It is half an hour of British documentary-movement drollery, made by a Brazilian in London for a government post office, with a German dancer in the cast, which is roughly what 1934 looks like from inside the emigration. It is also the last time a camera photographs her for thirty-one years. The next director to film her is Fellini.
sources: arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert' (screening Pett and Pott, 6 July 2026)
suggested_refs: Alberto Cavalcanti's GPO Film Unit sound experiments, 1934

stops.name: London, the marriage that is a passport
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedias. The divorce from Helmuth von Krause was finalized on 23 November 1935 in Germany, five months earlier, and is attested on both.
stops.campa: Five months after the German divorce comes through, she marries the British writer and cultural organizer Robin Hay Anderson in London. What the marriage produces is a British passport. The passport is the reason she is alive in 1945 and out of Europe in 1940, and it is why the whole American chapter, the bar, the licence, the night in a Provincetown cell, is possible at all. Neither party discusses the marriage much afterwards, and the certificate is the only thing either of them keeps from it. She is forty-four.
suggested_refs: Robin Hay Anderson and the British protective marriages of the 1930s emigration

stops.name: Paris, Raymond Duncan's theatre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Gert's memoir. No independent source was reached for the performances or for the American manager's offer; no month is given and January is a placeholder. The coordinate is 31 Rue de Seine, Raymond Duncan's address. Isadora Duncan's journey file documents her brother's Greek-revival institute at Kopanos in Athens and neither corroborates a Paris venue nor mentions Gert.
stops.campa: She performs at the theatre of Raymond Duncan, Isadora's brother, who wears a hand-woven tunic and sandals in the Rue de Seine and has been running his own Hellenic academy there for thirty years. Gert threw out Isadora's Greek harmony as romantic before the last war, and is now working in the Greek harmony's front room, because it is a room and she needs one. An American manager sees her there and offers a round-trip ticket, a contract, and five hundred dollars.
sources: Gert's memoir, as summarized in the research dossier
isadora_duncan.journey.json (Raymond Duncan at Kopanos; no Paris venue, no Gert)
suggested_refs: Raymond Duncan's Akademia at 31 Rue de Seine, Paris

stops.name: New York, the French Line pier
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the memoir. The crossing aboard the Ile de France is dated to early 1939 in the dossier's judgement; some summaries put it in 1938, and the disagreement is not resolved. The month is set to February and is unattested. The coordinate is the French Line berth on the Hudson at West 48th Street.
stops.campa: The Ile de France puts her down at the French Line berth on the Hudson, at West Forty-eighth Street, with a contract she has not read closely, no English worth the name, and no working idea of how an American household budget is arranged. Germany is nine months from Poland and has stopped being a country she can go back to. She has been a famous person in Berlin since before most of this city's dancers were born. She is forty-seven, and the manager's five hundred dollars are already spent.
sources: Gert's memoir, as summarized in the research dossier
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests of the Ile de France, Compagnie Generale Transatlantique, 1938-39

stops.name: Santa Monica and Hollywood, not the type
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Gert's memoir; no month is given, June is a placeholder, and no independent source for any of it was reached. The stop is pinned at Salka Viertel's house on Mabery Road, Santa Monica; the Hollywood meetings folded into it have no located address.
stops.campa: She takes a bus across the continent to the one door in America she has a name for: Salka Viertel's house on Mabery Road, where the German film emigration eats on Sundays and jobs are found across a table. It gets her meetings and the meetings get her nothing. The producer Walter Wanger tells her she is not the type. She tells Ernst Lubitsch that American actors look like picture postcards, and the conversation ends there. Within the year she is washing dishes in Provincetown.
sources: Gert's memoir, as summarized in the research dossier
suggested_refs: Salka Viertel's Mabery Road salon and the Los Angeles film emigration

stops.name: Provincetown, the model at Hofmann's school
stops.date_confidence: the posing at Hans Hofmann's Provincetown school is attested on English Wikipedia; the rent, the wage, the sitting fee, and the account of what she did while posing come from Gert's memoir alone. No month is recorded and June is a placeholder.
stops.campa: A shed room at twenty-five dollars a month, dishes washed at thirty cents an hour, and then five mornings a week standing naked for Hans Hofmann's painting students at twelve dollars fifty the set. She will not simply hold a pose. She works through a sequence of theatrical postures, one after another, giving the coming abstract expressionists a performance nobody commissioned and nobody could sell tickets to. The dishwashing she files, in her own account, under American beginnings.
stops.quote: a classic beginning in America for everyone who wants to become a millionare
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Die Bettlerbar von New York, p. 10, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), pp. 51-52; the spelling is Mozingo's
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), pp. 51-52

stops.name: New York, the Cherry Lane Theatre
stops.date_confidence: the programme and the month are attested on English Wikipedia; the day is not recorded and is defaulted to the first. The account of the reviews is dossier-only and was not traced to a printed notice.
stops.campa: Thirty-eight Commerce Street, a hundred and eighty seats in a converted box on a bent Village street, and a programme of Boxen, Baby, Tod, Kupplerin, Koloratursaengerin. The boxer, the infant, the dying, the procuress, the coloratura. Reviewers admire Tod and find the rest too European, which is a polite way of saying they cannot work out whether she is joking. She is not joking. She has been performing Kupplerin, the old whore who has moved into management, for twenty years.
stops.quote: When the street walker grows old she stays in her profession. She is no longer able to execute her profession, she brings others together . . . . I showed a few typical movements of the procuror, how she makes her business, the joy of having achieved it and her drunkenness
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, 'Than by the Dynamic', p. 7, quoted in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 44
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 44
suggested_refs: The Cherry Lane Theatre, 38 Commerce Street, and its 1940 season

stops.name: Provincetown, the White Whale
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1941 on English Wikipedia; the month is set to July. Tennessee Williams's encouragement is attested there and rests ultimately on Gert's own account.
stops.campa: She performs at the White Whale and the European reputation, which was worth nothing at all in Hollywood, fills a Cape Cod bar for a season. Among the people who come in is a playwright from Mississippi, not yet famous, working summer jobs on the Cape. Tennessee Williams tells her she ought to open a cabaret in New York. She is forty-nine years old, broke, and has just spent a year as an artist's model and a dishwasher in this town, and she takes the advice.
stops.quote: I was possessed, as I had been possessed earlier by dance. It does not matter to the possessed, by what she is possessed. She is possessed by everything she does
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Die Bettlerbar von New York, p. 11, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 52
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 52
suggested_refs: The White Whale, Provincetown, summer 1941

stops.name: New York, 3 Morton Street: the Beggar Bar opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1941; the month is set to November and is not recorded. The address is 3 Morton Street at Bleecker. Tennessee Williams as waiter and reciter, Kadidja Wedekind and Maria Collm performing, and Judith Malina in the cloakroom are attested; Julian Beck, Jackson Pollock and Jack Kerouac appear in later accounts with no dates, jobs, or duration established anywhere, and are not carried here. Source failure recorded: kuenste-im-exil.de, the page behind much of this material, is currently unreachable, with DNS failure on www and 404 on the bare host.
stops.campa: A cellar on Morton Street at Bleecker, furnished entirely out of what she could beg for, which is where the name comes from and what she says about it. Tennessee Williams waits tables and recites. Kadidja Wedekind and Maria Collm perform. Judith Malina takes the coats. The room fills with emigres, painters, sailors on leave, Black patrons and gay patrons in a city that gave them few other rooms to sit down in. She is forty-nine, and she paints the walls herself.
stops.quote: Whoever runs a nightclub stands with one foot in jail. This industry is run through with gangsters and racketeers
stops.quote_source: A prospective investor's attorney, warning Gert while she was seeking financing, in Valeska Gert, Die Bettlerbar von New York, p. 115, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 55
sources: Kuenste im Exil, 'Valeska Gert: Beggar Bar' (site currently unreachable)
Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 55
suggested_refs: The Beggar Bar advertisement in Aufbau, 9 October 1942

stops.name: New York, the telephone calls she makes herself
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Gert's memoir, which is the only source for the calls; the month is set to December and is unattested. Nothing corroborates that investigators actually came.
stops.campa: The second night is empty. She telephones the Intelligence Bureau in her own unmistakable accent and reports that the German woman running the new cabaret on Morton Street is always stalking sailors and soldiers and is probably a Nazi spy. Then she telephones again, about the opium cigarettes. The woman she is denouncing is a Jewish refugee with a British passport, which is to say herself. Investigators arrive, and behind the investigators come the curious, and the room fills.
stops.quote: There is a new cabaret on Morton Street. The owner is German, she is always stalking sailors and soldiers . . . . She must be a Nazi spy
stops.quote_source: Gert's own account of the tip she telephoned in, Die Bettlerbar von New York, p. 32, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 58
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 58
suggested_refs: Valeska Gert, Die Bettlerbar von New York (arani, 1950)

stops.name: New York, the licence taken away
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: English Wikipedia gives February 1945, German Wikipedia gives spring 1945. February is used to hold segment order. The stated cause, loss of the cabaret licence after the alcoholic Beggar Sip, coffee mixed with egg liqueur, was served in a room with no liquor licence, could not be re-checked because kuenste-im-exil.de is unreachable, and is carried as reported.
stops.campa: She had been serving something called a Beggar Sip, coffee with egg liqueur in it, in a room licensed for no alcohol whatever. In the first months of 1945, February by one account and the spring by another, the cabaret licence is revoked and the bar closes. Three and a half years of a room she built out of begged furniture end in a municipal file. She does not describe it as a business failing, and the language she reaches for is not the language of commerce at all.
stops.quote: I woke at night from anxious dreams. I could not comprehend that my Beggar's Bar had been taken away. It had become my child. I had created it from nothing and fought for it like a lion. It had been murdered. It is not only murder when a person is killed. Bureaucrats and incompetent lawyers may destroy art—something very human. Because that was my cabaret.
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Die Bettlerbar von New York, p. 113, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 64
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 64
suggested_refs: New York City cabaret licensing under the wartime administration

stops.name: Provincetown, Valeska's and the night in jail
stops.date_confidence: the waterfront studio cabaret opening in May 1946 and the night in jail are attested in outline on English Wikipedia; the decor, the dispute over a dance partner's unpaid wages, and the release by regulars come from the memoir. The dossier itself flags that the docket and disposition of the contempt proceeding were never located.
stops.campa: A waterfront studio painted light blue under pink bulbs, stools cut down from nail barrels, a stage made of two crates the tide brought in. Fourteen months after New York took the last room away she has built another one out of what the beach provided. The neighbours complain about the noise and a dance partner complains about his wages. Held in contempt for refusing to pay the fine, she spends a night in a Provincetown cell, and the bar's regulars get her out in the morning. She is fifty-four. No court paper for any of it has ever been found.
stops.quote: All of my cabarets are true expressions of me. I gave them each full expression, in which they languished, and I always find an excuse to throw them away. . . . The authorities treated me miserably. It was related to the many false accusations, that always occurred with my cabarets.
stops.quote_source: Valeska Gert, Katze von Kampen, p. 97, translated in Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (PhD diss., Ohio State University, 2008), p. 59
sources: Karen A. Mozingo, Crossing the Borders of German and American Modernism (2008), p. 59
suggested_refs: Valeska Gert, Katze von Kampen

stops.name: Paris, waiting for a permit
stops.date_confidence: attested that she returned to Europe in 1947 and spent time in Paris and Zurich while seeking permission to enter Berlin; no month is recorded and January is a placeholder. The coordinate is the canonical Paris pin used across the atlas rather than a located address.
stops.campa: She comes back across the Atlantic and cannot get into Germany. Berlin is cut into four occupation sectors and entry runs on paper issued by armies, none of which owes anything to a fifty-five-year-old dancer with a British passport, a revoked American cabaret licence, and a repertoire nobody in either country has seen on a stage since 1932. Nine years earlier she had stood in this same city with a ticket out, and had taken it. Now she waits, in Paris first and then in Switzerland, and the wait runs into a second year.
sources: andre_breton.journey.json and isadora_duncan.journey.json (shared canonical Paris coordinate)
suggested_refs: Allied travel permits and re-entry into occupied Germany, 1947-48

stops.name: Zurich, Valeska and her kitchen staff
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1948 on English Wikipedia and described as running about half a year; no month is recorded, January is a placeholder, and no address is given by any source.
stops.campa: The cafe-cabaret is called Valeska und ihr Kuechenpersonal, Valeska and Her Kitchen Staff, and it runs about half a year in a city that spent the whole war intact and well fed. The joke in the title is the one she has been making since Morton Street: the performers are the help, the help are the performers, and the proprietor scrubs the floor herself after closing. Zurich is a waiting room with good coffee in it. She is watching the post for a permit.
suggested_refs: Zurich's wartime and postwar exile cabaret, from the Cabaret Cornichon onward

stops.name: Baden-Baden, six months' permission
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives a six-month permit from the American occupation authorities and December 1948, while English Wikipedia's summary places the entry in 1949. Not adjudicated; the earlier date is used to hold order.
stops.campa: She re-enters Germany through Baden-Baden on a six-month permit from an army of occupation, twenty-seven years after she danced Tanz in Orange out of her repertoire for the last time in this same spa town. The country she is being let back into for half a year is the country that expelled her, under new management, divided into zones and short of everything including coal. Six months is what the paper says. She does not linger in the south where it was stamped, and she does not treat the limit as binding. She goes straight to Berlin.
suggested_refs: American occupation-zone entry permits, 1948

stops.name: Berlin, Bei Valeska in the Opernkeller
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weaker than usually stated. Both Wikipedias report a cabaret Bei Valeska in the former Opernkeller of the Theater des Westens, but German Wikipedia's article on that building mentions no Opernkeller and no Bei Valeska, recording the Wilde Buehne and the Tingel-Tangel-Theater in the basement instead. The Staedtische Oper did occupy the house after 1945, so the siting is plausible and unsourced. No month, January a placeholder. Coordinate corrected to Kantstrasse 12, 52.5059, 13.3290.
stops.campa: In a cellar under the Theater des Westens, where the city opera has been playing since the war took its own house away, she opens Bei Valeska. Berlin outside is rubble with a two-month-old currency and an airlift passing over it every few minutes. The audience is the same city that filled the Kohlkopp in 1932, minus the ones who were killed and the ones who got out. She is fifty-seven, and Bei Valeska is the fifth room she has opened under her own name.
suggested_refs: The Theater des Westens, Kantstrasse 12, and its basement stages

stops.name: Berlin, the Hexenkueche
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1950 and running in winter seasons into the mid-1950s; no month is recorded, January is a placeholder, and no street address is given by any source.
stops.campa: The Witch's Kitchen runs through the winter seasons and keeps running into the mid-1950s. A young Klaus Kinski appears there and works there. The numbers go straight at what West Germany has agreed among itself not to discuss: she performs the KZ-Kommandeuse, the camp commandant's wife, Ilse Koch put on a cabaret stage a few years after the trial, in a small room, at small tables, for the price of the drinks. How the room took it, whether it laughed, is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Hexenkueche and West Berlin's early postwar cabaret

stops.name: Kampen auf Sylt, the Ziegenstall
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951 by both Wikipedias and by sylt.de; no month is recorded and January is a placeholder. Contradiction recorded rather than resolved: kabarett.de, affiliated with the Deutsches Tanzarchiv, dates the continuous run of the Ziegenstall from 1956, and whether that marks a later formalization is not established. Coordinate corrected to 54.954, 8.344.
stops.campa: She moves out of Berlin for good and turns the Sylt house into a bar called the Ziegenstall, the Goat Shed. Hay on the floor, milking stools to sit on, mangers along the wall. The waitresses sing and recite between rounds, which is the same arrangement she ran on Morton Street with different livestock. It opens with the season and shuts when the tourists go. She is fifty-nine when it opens and eighty-six when it shuts for the last time, twenty-seven years later, in the week she dies.
sources: kabarett.de, Valeska Gert profile (dating the run from 1956)
suggested_refs: The Ziegenstall, Kampen auf Sylt, 1951-1978

stops.name: Rome, Cinecitta: Fellini
stops.date_confidence: the casting in Giulietta degli spiriti is attested; the shooting site for her scenes is not, and Fellini shot location work elsewhere in the city, so the Cinecitta pin is an inference. Coordinate corrected to 41.8525, 12.5782; a figure of 41.8577, 12.5687 in circulation falls about 1 km west-northwest of the lot, in residential Don Bosco. No month, January a placeholder.
stops.campa: Thirty-one years after Pett and Pott, Federico Fellini puts her into Giulietta degli spiriti, among the mediums and household spirits crowding a bourgeois Roman wife's hallucination. She is seventy-three. A generation of filmgoers who have never sat through a Pabst silent meet her here first, in colour, as an apparition at the edge of somebody else's hallucination. Which of the Roman sets held her scenes is not established; Fellini shot part of the film away from Cinecitta.
sources: arsenal-berlin.de, 'A Tribute to Valeska Gert' (screening the film, 13 July 2026)
suggested_refs: Federico Fellini, Giulietta degli spiriti (1965)

stops.name: West Germany, the gold band and the television years
stops.date_confidence: the Filmband in Gold of 28 June 1970 and the 1973 guest role in Fassbinder's Acht Stunden sind kein Tag are attested. The talk-show appearance on Hansjuergen Rosenbauer's Je spaeter der Abend is carried at the commonly given date of 19 November 1975, which was not independently reconfirmed this pass, and the museum page that would corroborate Wolfgang Mueller's account of watching it now returns 404. The stop is dated to the award and pinned at the Berlin pin; the broadcasts have no single location.
stops.campa: The Filmband in Gold arrives in June 1970, for long-standing and outstanding contribution to German film, from the film industry that struck her name off its lists in 1933. Rainer Werner Fassbinder gives her a guest part in Acht Stunden sind kein Tag. She turns up on late-night television opposite a chat-show host, an old woman with a face that has been doing this since the Kaiser, and young people watching decide she is the first punk. That reading is made in 1975, and not by her.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Valeska Gert' (Filmband in Gold, 28 June 1970)
suggested_refs: Je spaeter der Abend, Hansjuergen Rosenbauer's talk show, broadcast of 19 November 1975

stops.name: West Germany, Der Fangschuss and the contract not filmed
stops.date_confidence: the role of Aunt Praskovia in Volker Schloendorff's Der Fangschuss (1976) and the contract of 1 March 1978 to play Knock in Werner Herzog's Nosferatu: Phantom der Nacht are both attested. No month for the film, January a placeholder. The stop is pinned at the Berlin pin; the film's shooting locations are not established here.
stops.campa: Volker Schloendorff casts her as Aunt Praskovia in Der Fangschuss, and it is the last fiction film she finishes. On the first of March 1978 she signs with Werner Herzog to play Knock, the estate agent who sells the vampire his house and ends up eating flies in a cell. She is eighty-six and has been handed a part in a German film about a plague arriving from the east and settling into a town that thought it was safe. She dies before the cameras turn.
suggested_refs: Werner Herzog, Nosferatu: Phantom der Nacht (1979), for which the role of Knock was recast

stops.name: Kampen auf Sylt, the cat at the door
stops.date_confidence: the death date is not fixed and the sources disagree. German Wikipedia gives between 15 and 18 March 1978, probably 16 March; kabarett.de gives the same range; filmportal.de gives 15 March. The most probable date is used here. Police forced entry on 18 March after she had not been seen for four days. The medical cause of death is not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: She dies alone in the house beside the Ziegenstall, somewhere inside the four days between the fifteenth and the eighteenth of March, and nobody has established which. The season has not opened; the bar is shut and the village is empty. A neighbour hears the cat crying behind the door and calls the police, who force it on the eighteenth and find her. What she died of is not recorded anywhere. She had said she wanted a bright red coffin. The funeral uses an ordinary one with a red cloth laid over it.
suggested_refs: The Gert house and the Ziegenstall site at Kampen, later inherited by Werner Hoefer and demolished

stops.name: Berlin, Friedhof Ruhleben, field XVI-175
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Friedhof Ruhleben, Am Hain, Berlin-Westend, in field XVI-175, and the Ehrengrab status granted in 1978, are attested verbatim on German Wikipedia; the exact burial date is not established and April is a placeholder. Coordinate corrected to 52.5236, 13.2299 from the cemetery's own article; two other points in circulation for this one grave, 52.5187 / 13.2601 and 52.5219 / 13.2178, are wrong by 850 m and 2.1 km respectively. Volker Schloendorff giving the funeral address is dossier-only and unconfirmed.
stops.campa: Berlin was the city she said she was born in and meant to die in, and she gets half of it. Field sixteen, plot one hundred and seventy-five, a black stone with her name written across it in pink, the letters copying her own signature, and beneath the name one word: Taenzerin. Dancer. Not actress, not cabaret proprietor, not the woman who ran the Beggar Bar and lost it to a licensing clerk. The city that shut her out in 1933 makes the plot an honorary grave in the same year it puts her in it.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Valeska Gert' (field number, lettering, Ehrengrab, red cloth)
suggested_refs: Gert's papers at the Archiv der Akademie der Kuenste, Berlin, placed there by the Erbengemeinschaft through Frank-Manuel Peter
